Question: A painting \(18''\times24''\) is to be placed into a wooden frame with the longer dimension vertical. The wood at the top and bottom is twice as wide as the wood on the sides. If the frame area equals that of the painting itself, the ratio of the smaller to the larger dimension of the framed painting is:
Solution:
The painting is \(18\) inches wide and \(24\) inches tall. Since the wood and painting have equal areas, the outside rectangle must have the area of two paintings. This suggests building a suitable rectangle from two copies of the painting.

Place the copies one above the other, each with its \(24\)-inch side horizontal. Together they form a rectangle \(24\) inches wide and \(36\) inches tall.

Center the original painting inside this proposed outside rectangle. Each side border then has width
\[
\frac{24-18}{2}=3\text{ inches},
\]
while each top or bottom border has width
\[
\frac{36-24}{2}=6\text{ inches}.
\]
Thus the top and bottom borders are twice as wide as the side borders. Also, removing the painting from a rectangle with twice its area leaves exactly one painting's area of wood, as required.

This is the only possible frame size. Wider side borders would require wider top and bottom borders, increasing both outside dimensions and therefore the area. Narrower borders would decrease both dimensions and the area. Neither could give the same required area.

The ratio of the smaller outside dimension to the larger is therefore
\[
24:36=\boxed{2:3},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
